title: Who Was the Man in the Iron Mask? A Bastille Record Says Black Velvet
description:
The Bastille's 1703 record describes a black velvet mask. So why did later generations call him the Man in the Iron Mask? This episode follows a 1669 official letter, a 1698 admission record, and a 1703 death entry through Voltaire's letter and later fiction, separating what the records say from later theories and an identity that remains unknown.

Only if the masked prisoner was the Dauger named in the 1669 letter do the four prisons and roughly 34 years of captivity fit. That is a duration of imprisonment, not mask-wearing. The royal twin is a later tale. Information current to 2026-10-14. Illustrations were generated with AI; sources for the historical records are listed in the description.

14595114.text: In July 1698, Saint-Mars received another transfer order.

43592117.text: One transcription reads it as Marchioly.

67729286.text: That error warns us: a writer's account cannot replace prison records.

83845803.text: Was this 'old prisoner' Dauger? The order is silent.

f882011e.text: In 1703, a Bastille deputy recorded the death of a masked prisoner.

780680cf.text: He noted the time of death and the mask, but no name to prove who he was.

036c0187.text: In 1669, an official letter named a prisoner held under tight guard.

bb259d67.text: Was that the name missing from the deputy's entry?

dfc7a42b.text: In 1698, a governor brought an old prisoner into the Bastille.

db81d592.text: What did the admission record call this prisoner?

bdea9e04.text: In 1738, Voltaire gave this story a new name in a letter.

4bc41163.text: What would his words turn the mask into?

27099bdc.text: Who was buried, and was his mask really made of iron?

48ba5712.text: The deputy did not stop at the word 'masked'.

bced8458.text: The death entry said the mask was black velvet.

45164df0.text: He recorded the prisoner's death at about 10 p.m. that night.

349f207c.text: At 4 p.m. the next day, he was buried in Saint-Paul parish cemetery.

30d6e64a.text: You'd think the burial record proves who he was.

d9c5bfdb.text: Instead, it left a name whose spelling even varies.

18bcd1aa.text: Another copy reads Marchialy. The deputy's margin has a third spelling.

97c8ed9d.text: These readings concern the burial, but none proves his real name.

172c4b5f.text: Whom did the earlier letter to the governor name?

446cb5b5.text: On July 19, 1669, that letter named Eustache Dauger.

067878ed.text: It was sent by Louvois to prison governor Saint-Mars.

0b26481a.text: The king ordered him held at Pignerol.

712867ca.text: The letter alone does not tell us his crime.

a7a7e3bb.text: Yet it even specified who brought his food.

22215fc5.text: Saint-Mars had to bring food; guards must not hear Dauger speak.

adbdfb65.text: Nor could he send word outside.

836e3743.text: What did they fear he'd reveal?

6e0e8bfb.text: The letter gives no answer, only a term later readers struggled to explain.

4770a975.text: Some read it literally; a scholar sees a pun.

e6345955.text: More crucially, the letter says nothing of a mask.

8dffdb67.text: Nor does it say Dauger was the nameless Bastille prisoner.

7c22ba05.text: The first record gives no name; the secret order does.

6e55055d.text: Is there a clue that can link the two ends to one name?

ec1ee0f4.text: It let him take an 'old prisoner' from Sainte-Marguerite to the Bastille.

e690a274.text: He was told to keep others from seeing or identifying the prisoner.

5bc42258.text: It covers this transfer, not security at each earlier prison.

7355e817.text: On September 18 that year, the Bastille entry picks up the trail.

300c617e.text: It gives no name or material; black velvet appears in the death entry.

4ee87957.text: The deputy also noted that Saint-Mars had held him at Pignerol.

e1f6363c.text: The same governor and old prison offer a possible link between the records.

e99ebdf1.text: A lead invites inquiry; it is not a signed identity.

1ccb3806.text: Later, a letter gave the mask a different name.

f8262028.text: Did that word really name the mask's material?

4d151adf.text: In 1738, Voltaire called him 'the man in the iron mask,' citing no material test.

3282e1f7.text: He said he asked former attendants.

08402cf6.text: But the letter has no transcript.

5df72cd6.text: So we cannot tell what mask that person saw firsthand.

a35852ed.text: Nor can we conclude Voltaire was the first to say 'iron'.

22c31821.text: The death entry said black velvet. How did 'iron' overtake it?

a2e86117.text: In 1751, The Age of Louis XIV spread the story.

a0b99b19.text: Voltaire wrote of steel springs at the chin, letting the prisoner eat in his mask.

a1d34f98.text: He said the springs were steel; that does not prove the whole mask was iron.

f010cca9.text: The book added vivid details that brought the nameless man to life.

458d1f68.text: But it dates his move to the Bastille to 1690.

42fdf9fe.text: The prison's entry is eight years later.

3a052062.text: In later tellings, the mask grew harder, and his origins grew nobler.

19cabd14.text: When did royal blood enter the story?

1648d74e.text: A passage in a 1771 edition guessed he was the king's elder brother.

7e41df5a.text: It is labeled an 'editor's addition'; whether Voltaire wrote it is disputed.

59982a41.text: A later guess; the prison never disclosed his ancestry.

d357e078.text: By the late 18th century, the brother story spawned a twin version.

065e2185.text: With identical faces, hiding one makes the plot work.

4ecf1ae5.text: Dumas later wrote the twins into a novel, tying the mask more tightly to royalty.

85100ec0.text: The tale grew fuller; the first records still say nothing of royalty.

22b75408.text: Metal hoods and twins explain how the legend spread, not the prisoner's name.

143be677.text: The best leads: the secret order and copies of the burial record.

baeadea2.text: Put the two documents side by side: the crucial gap appears in the names.

029cafbf.text: The spelling in the burial copy does not match Dauger in the secret order.

ec47a1b6.text: If Dauger was the masked prisoner, the governor's route would connect.

5d60fd05.text: From Pignerol to Exilles, Sainte-Marguerite, and the Bastille.

f5c35d28.text: Four prisons and about 34 years follow only if that identity is right.

ca6f2073.text: Those years mean captivity, not time in a mask.

63748dc9.text: But the death entry omits Dauger; scholars infer the link.

e8d89ffb.text: Historian Sonnino proposed a motive for silence.

40285df9.text: He thinks Dauger served Cardinal Mazarin's financial steward.

f409b936.text: He thinks Dauger may have known Mazarin stole a former English king and queen's assets.

6c44c3b1.text: As the French king urged England's king into war, this could cause trouble.

5438f7da.text: Sonnino reads the letter and politics this way; the order names no crime.

d50d4573.text: It may explain secrecy, but cannot name the man in the death entry.

ef2940a1.text: But if the burial name points elsewhere, can Dauger's route still stand?

13f0cb04.text: Another lead is the burial name we saw earlier.

87ab87c4.text: The parish book is lost; 19th-century printed copies survive.

5c6e9a3e.text: We can compare copies and transcripts, but not confirm that was his real name.

14d8d94f.text: The 19th-century historian Funck-Brentano linked the name to Mattioli.

168efb94.text: That makes Mattioli a candidate; it does not end the dispute.

30fb8aac.text: If he was Mattioli, we cannot give him Dauger's prison route.

ceb3f543.text: Each theory has clues; combining them creates a man no document describes.

c7a67f2d.text: The Iron Mask Museum in Cannes still says his identity is unknown.

1fb84766.text: What surviving object could test the word 'iron'?

926246b2.text: No mask survives to test Voltaire's 'iron'; rival identity theories remain.

9fda69c0.text: Had you heard of the records or the twin tale?

7bd9eb2a.text: If you enjoy mysteries traced through records, subscribe to 奇聞檔案局.
